hero.heading: Learn How to Practice. Then Hear the Difference.
hero.problem: You can play it at home. Then the lesson comes and it falls apart. You were told to practice more. Nobody showed you how.
hero.solution: The Practice Code is a seven-element method for any instrument: accurate from the first note, clear targets instead of clock-watching, and practice that holds up when you perform.

first-steps.description: The Practice Code: First Steps is the starter book for beginners and their parents: the first habits of good music practice, made simple.
first-steps.heading: Start Practicing the Right Way From the Very First Week
first-steps.lead: The first months decide whether practice becomes a habit or a daily argument. First Steps gives beginners, and the parents helping them, a few simple habits that make every session count.

stakes.heading: Beginners Are Told to Practice. Few Are Shown How.
stakes.text: So they play the piece through, mistakes and all, until the timer goes. Progress slows and practice turns into a chore.
items: Playing the whole piece through, mistakes and all
Watching the clock until the 20 minutes are up
"Go and do your practice" becoming a daily argument
Parents who want to help but don't play themselves

items.title: Get It Right First
items.text: Play slowly enough to play it correctly. Then play it right five more times.

items.title: Aim for a Target, Not a Time
items.text: "Play bars 1 to 4 perfectly" beats "practice for 20 minutes" every time.

items.title: Practice After, Not At
items.text: Hang practice on something that already happens, like getting home from school.

items.title: Look Back Before You Move On
items.text: Start each session with yesterday's work, so it is still there tomorrow.

items.title: Make It a Game
items.text: Simple practice games that reward getting it right, not getting it done.

items.title: For Parents
items.text: How to help when you don't play yourself, and what to say instead of "go and practice".

book.description: The Practice Code by Simon Horsey: seven elements that turn practice into progress on any musical instrument, at any level.
book.audience: For students ready for the full method
book.heading: The Practice Code: Seven Elements That Turn Practice Into Progress
book.lead: Your lesson is not where you learn the most each week. Your practice is. The Practice Code shows you exactly what to do with that time, on any instrument, at any level.

stakes.heading: More Practice Is Not the Answer
stakes.text: The 30-minute rule teaches you to watch the clock. Meanwhile your brain learns whatever you repeat, mistakes included.
items: Practicing by the clock instead of to a target
Repeating a mistake until it becomes a habit
Pieces that work at home and fall apart in the lesson
Learned it yesterday, can't play it today
Leaving dynamics and expression until "later"

offer.heading: Seven Elements. One Method.

items.title: The Accuracy Protocol
items.text: Right from the first note. Slow enough to be 100% correct, then five more times to lock it in.

items.title: Target-Oriented Systems
items.text: Swap "practice for 30 minutes" for clear targets you can tick off. Stop when you hit them.

items.title: Strategic Segmentation
items.text: Break music into small, overlapping sections so the joins never trip you up.

items.title: Active Listening
items.text: Train your ear while you play: tone, attack, intonation, and what a recording really tells you.

items.title: Environment and Mindset
items.text: Set up your space and your thinking so nothing gets between you and the work.

items.title: Systematic Review
items.text: Review at the right intervals, so what you learn this week is still there next month.

items.title: Performance Integration
items.text: Practice what you will perform: expression, tempo and pressure, built in from the start.

includes: The Accuracy Health Check: measure how effective your practice is in one week
Practice games, including Target Dice and Practice Chess
Notes for parents on supporting practice at home
offer.includes_review: Taken from draft V3.2 of the book. Confirm the final contents, length and format.

steps.title: Take the Accuracy Health Check
steps.text: Track one week of practice and see where you are starting from.

steps.title: Add One Element at a Time
steps.text: Give each element a couple of weeks to become automatic before adding the next.

steps.title: Hear the Difference
steps.text: Your pieces hold together in lessons and on stage, because that is how you practiced them.

faqs.a: Any instrument and any style. The method is about how you practice, not what you play.

faqs.q: What level do I need to be?
faqs.a: Any level. Beginners build good habits from the start, and advanced players apply the same seven elements to harder music.

faqs.q: Should I start with First Steps instead?
faqs.a: If you or your child are in the first year or two of playing, First Steps is the gentler way in. The Practice Code covers the same ground and goes much further.

faqs.q: Is this a new edition of Practice Makes Perfect?
faqs.a: Yes. The Practice Code is the rewritten and renamed successor to Practice Makes Perfect, reorganised around seven elements.

faqs.q: I'm a parent, not a musician. Will it help?
faqs.a: Yes. There is a section written for parents on how to support practice at home.

book.closing: Stop Counting Minutes. Start Hitting Targets.

academy.audience: For musicians who want to go further
academy.heading: See Every Element in Action, Then Go Deeper
academy.lead: The book gives you the method. The course shows it to you at the instrument, then takes on the hard parts: memorizing, sight-reading and playing under pressure.

stakes.heading: Knowing the Method Is Not the Same as Using It
stakes.text: Most people read a good idea, try it for a week and slide back into old habits. Seeing it done, step by step, is what makes it stick.
items: Reading about a technique but never quite applying it
Not being sure you are doing it right
Getting stuck on memorizing, sight-reading or nerves
Having nobody to ask between lessons
